Nowhere did I find a really clear space for sketching until this occasion when I prolonged beyond the proper limit the process of lying on my back in bed. Then the light of that white heaven broke upon my vision, that breadth of mere white which is indeed almost the definition of Paradise, since it means purity and also means freedom. But alas! like all heavens, now that it is seen it is found to be unattainable; it looks more austere and more distant than the blue sky outside the window. For my proposal to paint on it with the bristly end of a broom has been discouraged—never mind by whom; by a person debarred from all political rights—and even my minor proposal to put the other end of the broom into the kitchen fire and turn it to charcoal has not been conceded. Yet I am certain that it was from persons in my position that all the original inspiration came for covering the ceilings of palaces and cathedrals with a riot of fallen angels or victorious gods. I am sure that it was only because Michael Angelo was engaged in the ancient and honourable occupation of lying in bed that he ever realized how the roof of the Sistine Chapel might be made into an awful imitation of a divine drama that could only be acted in the heavens.

The tone now commonly taken toward the practice of lying in bed is hypocritical and unhealthy. Of all the marks of modernity that seem to mean a kind of decadence, there is none more menacing and dangerous than the exultation of very small and secondary matters of conduct at the expense of very great and primary ones, at the expense of eternal ties and tragic human morality. If there is one thing worse than the modern weakening of major morals, it is the modern strengthening of minor morals. Thus it is considered more withering to accuse a man of bad taste than of bad ethics. Cleanliness is not next to godliness nowadays, for cleanliness is made essential and godliness is regarded as an offence. A playwright can attack the institution of marriage so long as he does not misrepresent the manners of society, and I have met Ibsenite pessimists who thought it wrong to take beer but right to take prussic acid. Especially this is so in matters of hygiene; notably such matters as lying in bed. Instead of being regarded, as it ought to be, as a matter of personal convenience and adjustment, it has come to be regarded by many as if it were a part of essential morals to get up early in the morning. It is upon the whole part of practical wisdom; but there is nothing good about it or bad about its opposite.

message.content:
During my search for a suitable environment to sketch, I stumbled upon an unexpected moment of inspiration while lying in bed longer than usual. In that instance, the brilliance of a vast white expanse flooded my sight, an embodiment of purity and liberty that could aptly represent a vision of Paradise. However, as with all idealized heavens, once perceived, it appeared more remote and forbidding than the serene blue sky just outside my window. My ambition to create art on that pristine canvas using the coarse end of a broom has met with disapproval—though the source of this objection remains irrelevant, stemming from an individual stripped of all political rights. Even my modest suggestion to transform the broom’s other end into charcoal by placing it in the kitchen fire has been rejected. Still, I firmly believe that those in my situation have historically sparked the creativity needed to embellish the ceilings of grand palaces and cathedrals with extravagant depictions of fallen angels or triumphant deities. I am convinced that it was during his own moments of repose that Michelangelo conceived the magnificent vision that led to the creation of the awe-inspiring ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, an imitation of celestial drama meant to be portrayed in the heavens.

The contemporary perspective on the act of resting in bed is often insincere and detrimental. Among the hallmarks of modernity that signal a decline in values, none is as alarming as the elevation of trivial behaviors over significant ethical principles, undermining essential human connections and the weight of profound moral dilemmas. The current trend of prioritizing minor faults over more consequential ethical breaches is troubling. It has become more shameful to accuse someone of lacking taste than to call out their moral failings. Cleanliness, once thought to be next to divinity, has shifted in meaning; it is now deemed obligatory, while spirituality may be viewed as a liability. A playwright may critique the institution of marriage, provided he accurately reflects societal norms, and I have encountered Ibsenite pessimists who deem it acceptable to consume prussic acid while condemning the act of drinking beer. This skewed perception is particularly evident in discussions surrounding hygiene, especially regarding the act of lying in bed. Rather than being seen as a matter of personal preference and comfort, many now treat the expectation of rising early as a moral imperative. While it can be argued that waking early embodies a form of practical wisdom, neither it nor its opposite carries intrinsic moral weight.
